subject: math
intro: A statistical question anticipates variability in the data used to answer it, so its answer comes from a distribution of values gathered across many individuals or observations. A non-statistical question has a single, fixed answer with no variability. Choose the single best answer for each question.

items.prompt:
Which of the following is a statistical question?
A) How old am I?
B) How tall are the students in our 6th grade class?
C) How many days are in one week?
D) What is the number of wheels on a bicycle?
items.answer: B) How tall are the students in our 6th grade class?

steps: A statistical question anticipates variability, meaning the answers vary from one individual to another and form a distribution.
Choice B asks about the heights of many students. Different students have different heights, so the answers vary. This is statistical.
Choice A asks about one specific person (me), so it has one fixed answer. Not statistical.
Choice C has the single fixed answer 7. Choice D has the single fixed answer 2. Each is one fixed fact, so neither is statistical, even though they involve numbers.
solution.answer: B) How tall are the students in our 6th grade class?

items.prompt:
Which of the following is NOT a statistical question?
A) How many pets does each student in our class own?
B) What are the shoe sizes of the players on the soccer team?
C) How old is the principal of our school?
D) How many hours of sleep did each member of my family get last night?
items.answer: C) How old is the principal of our school?

steps: A non-statistical question has one fixed answer with no variability.
Choice C asks about one specific person, the principal. One person has one age, so there is a single fixed answer. This is NOT statistical.
Choices A, B, and D each ask about a group (students, players, family members), and the answers vary across individuals, forming a distribution. Those are statistical.
solution.answer: C) How old is the principal of our school?

items.prompt:
Why is 'How many minutes did each student in the class spend reading last night?' a statistical question?
A) Because it contains the word 'minutes', which is a number.
B) Because different students spent different amounts of time, so the answers vary.
C) Because the answer is a single correct number.
D) Because it is a question about students, who are people.
items.answer: B) Because different students spent different amounts of time, so the answers vary.

steps: A question is statistical when it anticipates variability, that is, when the answers are expected to differ across individuals.
Choice B is correct: different students read for different amounts of time, so the answers vary and form a distribution.
Choice A is wrong because simply containing a number does not make a question statistical; what matters is variability in the answers.
Choice C is wrong because a statistical question produces many varying values, not a single fixed answer.
Choice D is wrong because being about people is not the reason; a question about one specific person would have no variability.
solution.answer: B) Because different students spent different amounts of time, so the answers vary.

items.prompt:
Which question is statistical, even though it does not use the words 'average', 'mean', or 'data'?
A) How many sides does a hexagon have?
B) How many pets does each student in the class have?
C) What year did our school open?
D) How many minutes are in one hour?
items.answer: B) How many pets does each student in the class have?

steps: A question does not need to say 'average' or 'data' to be statistical; it only needs to anticipate variability in the answers.
Choice B asks how many pets EACH student has. Different students own different numbers of pets, so the per-student answers vary. This is statistical.
Choice A has the single fixed answer 6, choice C names one fixed year, and choice D has the single fixed answer 60. Each has one fixed answer with no variability, so none of them is statistical.
solution.answer: B) How many pets does each student in the class have?

items.prompt:
Diego says 'What are the weights of the apples in this basket?' is NOT a statistical question because the apples are all the same kind. Is Diego correct, and why?
A) Yes, because apples of the same kind all weigh exactly the same.
B) Yes, because the question does not mention finding an average.
C) No, because the apples have different weights, so the answers vary and form a distribution.
D) No, because any question about objects is automatically statistical.
items.answer: C) No, because the apples have different weights, so the answers vary and form a distribution.

steps: Even apples of the same kind do not weigh exactly the same; their individual weights vary from apple to apple.
Choice C is correct: because the weights vary across the apples, the answers form a distribution, so the question IS statistical and Diego is wrong.
Choice A is wrong because identical-looking objects still have measurable variability in weight.
Choice B is wrong because a question does not need to mention 'average' to be statistical.
Choice D is wrong because not every question about objects is statistical; a question about one object would have no variability.
solution.answer: C) No, because the apples have different weights, so the answers vary and form a distribution.

items.prompt:
For the statistical question 'What are the daily high temperatures in our town this month?', what is the population being investigated and what kind of answer is expected?
A) The population is the single hottest day, and the answer is one temperature.
B) The population is the days of the month, and the answer is a distribution of varying temperatures.
C) The population is the town, and the answer is one average temperature with no variability.
D) The population is the thermometer, and the answer is a single fixed reading.
items.answer: B) The population is the days of the month, and the answer is a distribution of varying temperatures.

steps: The question collects a high temperature for each day this month, so the group being studied (the population) is the set of days in the month.
Choice B is correct: the data are one high temperature per day, and those values vary from day to day, forming a distribution.
Choice A is wrong because the question asks about all the days, not only the single hottest day.
Choice C is wrong because the data themselves vary even if you later compute an average; the variability is in the daily readings.
Choice D is wrong because the population is the days observed, not the measuring instrument.
solution.answer: B) The population is the days of the month, and the answer is a distribution of varying temperatures.

items.prompt:
Which choice correctly rewrites the non-statistical question 'How many pages are in my math textbook?' as a statistical question?
A) How many pages are in the math textbooks used across the 6th grade?
B) How many pages are in my math textbook right now?
C) Is my math textbook longer than 100 pages?
D) What is the title of my math textbook?
items.answer: A) How many pages are in the math textbooks used across the 6th grade?

steps: The original asks about one specific book, so it has a single fixed answer and is not statistical. To make it statistical, the new question must anticipate variability across a group.
Choice A asks about the page counts of MANY textbooks across the 6th grade. Different books have different page counts, so the answers vary and form a distribution. This is statistical.
Choice B still asks about one specific textbook, so the answer is a single fixed number; not statistical.
Choice C asks one yes/no question about a single book, giving one fixed answer; not statistical.
Choice D asks for one fixed title of one book; not statistical.
solution.answer: A) How many pages are in the math textbooks used across the 6th grade?

items.prompt:
Maya claims 'Do the students in our grade like pizza?' cannot be statistical because a yes/no question has no numbers. Which response correctly evaluates her claim?
A) Maya is right, because statistical questions must produce numbers, not yes or no answers.
B) Maya is right, because the answer to a yes/no question is always a single fixed value.
C) Maya is wrong, because different students answer differently, so the yes and no responses vary and form a distribution.
D) Maya is wrong, because every question about a grade is automatically statistical.
items.answer: C) Maya is wrong, because different students answer differently, so the yes and no responses vary and form a distribution.

steps: Whether a question is statistical depends on anticipated variability in the answers, not on whether the answers are numbers.
Choice C is correct: across the grade, some students answer yes and others answer no, so the responses vary and form a distribution. The question IS statistical.
Choices A and B are wrong because yes/no responses can still vary from student to student, which is exactly the variability that makes a question statistical.
Choice D is wrong because not every question about a grade is statistical; a question about one fixed fact of the grade would have no variability.
solution.answer: C) Maya is wrong, because different students answer differently, so the yes and no responses vary and form a distribution.
